transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-03-21 09:32 UTC, duration ~48 minutes. Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marcus Vela (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Novus Lead ML Eng), Caleb Ortiz (Novus Platform Eng), Marta Lin (Novus Security).

Automatic summary (auto): quick onboarding lab focused on SDK auth, env variables, batching config for cost/latency trade-offs; agreed to POC kickoff next week and follow up on security docs.

00:00 Lena Park: okay, good morning everyone, thanks for taking the time. quick intro — i'm lena with Redwood, ae on the account. today we'll run a short onramp lab — focus on SDK auth, environment setup for python and typescript, and an example batching profile for your inference workload.
00:12 Priya Rao: morning — we just wanna make sure this maps to our CI and token rotation, and see how batching affects our 100ms latency targets.
00:22 Marcus Vela: yeah, i'll take the technical walkthrough. i'm marcus from redwood se — i'll demo the python quickstart, then switch to the ts client, show env var patterns, then a sample batching policy and how to surface metrics in console.
00:35 Caleb Ortiz: quick note, we run things in GKE private clusters behind egress nat, and our secrets live in Vault. also we have strict outbound firewall rules.
00:45 Marta Lin: and security's concerned about KMS integration and audit logs — SOC 2 compliance checks.

01:02 Marcus Vela: got it. to start, the simplest auth: an api key set as environment variable REDWOOD_API_KEY. we'll show a few patterns: local dev env, ci secrets, and vault + k8s external secrets.
01:18 Marcus Vela: (typing) python snippet: from redwood import Client; client = Client(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY')) — basic. in ts: import { Redwood } from '@redwood-inference/sdk'; const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY });
01:38 Priya Rao: are there options for short-lived tokens or oidc exchange?
01:43 Marcus Vela: yes — we support token exchange via our private deployment token broker or you can mint short-lived tokens using our hosted token API. for private deployments you can plug an oidc provider and our agent will exchange for ephemeral keys. we have sample helm charts for that.
01:58 Lena Park: note — we'll send the token broker doc after the call.

02:12 Marcus Vela: next, environment setup. dev: local .env with REDWOOD_API_KEY for dev. staging/prod: we recommend k8s secrets or cloud kms-protected secret in CI and inject at deploy time. example: CI pipeline uses gcloud secrets access and sets REDWOOD_API_KEY in runner env. if you're using vault, run a preflight sidecar that writes to file and set client to read from file path.
02:40 Caleb Ortiz: our CI rotates tokens hourly, that might be an issue if the sdk caches client instances for long-lived processes, how do we handle rotation?
02:49 Marcus Vela: good question. the python SDK supports a credential provider interface. you can implement a small refresh handler that reads secret on demand every N minutes or listens for file change and refreshes the internal header. in node sdk we have a refreshCallback option. i'll paste examples.
03:05 Priya Rao: hmm ok. can we limit the permissions on the tokens to inference-only? we need separation of duties.
03:11 Marcus Vela: yes, tokens can be scoped by role — inference-only keys, admin keys, billing keys. recommend inference-only for runtime.

03:28 Marcus Vela: moving to the quickstart project. i'm sharing a sandbox link in chat (sandbox.redwood.dev/novus-345) — includes a pre-provisioned model and example repo. i'll walk through the repo layout: /python/quickstart.py, /ts/examples/chat.ts, ci/ pipeline.yaml, and samples/batching.json.
03:52 Lena Park: note — the sandbox has telemetry we can view in the console.

04:05 Marcus Vela: demo: python quickstart — launching. (audio: keys) first step pip install redwood-sdk, then set REDWOOD_API_KEY and run quickstart. quickstart will create a chat session and stream tokens.
04:26 Speaker 1: okay uh — streaming looks good, oh — sorry wrong screen for a sec.
04:34 Marcus Vela: (laughs) no worries. you'll see stream chunks arrive; we show per-token latency in the console.
04:42 Priya Rao: in terms of cost — how does streaming affect token billing? token-based as usual; streaming doesn't change unit cost but may allow earlier render to user which impacts perceived latency.
04:56 Marcus Vela: exactly. also if you use prefix caching (we can enable at route level) repeated prompts will hit cache and reduce tokens charged.

05:10 Marcus Vela: now ts client: npm install @redwood-inference/sdk; set env var; run ts-node chat.ts. same behavior. note types provided. we try to keep parity between python and ts.
05:28 Caleb Ortiz: do we have typed interfaces for streaming events in ts to integrate with our frontend websocket?
05:33 Marcus Vela: yes, we emit chunk events and a final event — you can wire to your socket. sample integration in examples/websocket.ts.

06:01 Marcus Vela: ok batching. you mentioned 100ms p95 target. batching helps throughput but increases response latency per request. here's a sample batching.json we recommend for interactive agents: {"max_batch_size": 8, "max_wait_ms": 25, "prioritize_latency": true}. this keeps extra wait under 25ms and modest batch sizes.
06:28 Priya Rao: 25ms wait seems okay. our users tolerate up to 120ms, but p95 should be <200ms.
06:34 Marcus Vela: with that config and a model like redwood-medium-1 you'll likely see cost drop ~30% at your request rate. for stricter 50ms targets we can shift to smaller batch sizes and enable warm KV cache to lower token generation time.
06:50 Priya Rao: what's KV cache?
06:53 Marcus Vela: it's our prefix caching for autoregressive models — it keeps recent key/value states for common prefixes to avoid recomputing. very effective for agents with repeated system prompt or instruction templates.

07:10 Marta Lin: on the security side, can audit logs be exported to our splunk/stack?
07:15 Marcus Vela: yes — console exposes audit logs and you can configure sinks to push to cloud logging or an S3-compatible store. for private deployments we mount logs to your internal logging pipeline.
07:25 Marta Lin: and encryption at rest?
07:27 Lena Park: we support KMS integration and HSM for private deployments; hosted service encrypts using our KMS, and you can bring-your-own-key for private.

07:45 Marcus Vela: demo — switching to console. (screen share) on the left you can see routes, models, batching profiles, and telemetry. here's a route called "novus-chat" with model pinned to redwood-medium-1 and batching profile attached. you can edit and rollout canary.
08:10 Priya Rao: can we have region-based routing? some requests must stay in eu-west.
08:15 Marcus Vela: yes — policy routing can route by geo tag; for private you can enforce VPC-only. we'll show region pinning in the config.

08:28 Marcus Vela: now metrics — per-route p50/p95 latency, cost per 1k tokens, and queue depth. the export shows token-level breakdown.
08:40 Caleb Ortiz: is there an api for metrics? we'd like to ingest into our monitoring.
08:44 Marcus Vela: yep, metrics API and ingestion via prometheus exporter for on-prem. hosted has prometheus pushgateway integration as well.

09:05 Lena Park: quick pause — any blockers so far?
09:09 Priya Rao: main blocker is network egress policy and how sandbox will reach hosted endpoints. we prefer to run a private deployment but first want to validate on hosted with synthetic traffic.
09:20 Marcus Vela: we can provide a low-priv test subnet for egress via a small connector; or you can run a temporary proxy in your cluster. both options documented in the network setup guide.

09:38 Marcus Vela: now a short run of the batching POC. i'm going to run a synthetic load: 200 rps of small prompts with batching profile A (max_wait 25ms). (pause) you can see concurrent batch sizes avg ~6, p95 latency 140ms, cost per token reduced.
10:10 Priya Rao: can we reproduce that on our staging? what's the harness?
10:15 Marcus Vela: we use a simple locust script or k6 script that issues REST requests to the route. i'll attach the script.
10:22 Lena Park: note — attaching to followup.

10:35 Speaker 2: small crosstalk, Caleb: what about models and quantization?
10:38 Marcus Vela: good — we have quantized model variants hosted that reduce GPU memory and unit cost. for latency-sensitive workloads we have slightly larger unquantized variants. Optimize will recommend quantization profile based on evals.
10:52 Priya Rao: how automatic are those recommendations? do you run evals on our prompt set?
10:56 Marcus Vela: yes — in POC we can run a prompt set eval (you provide 200–500 prompts) and Optimize will recommend model + quantization + batching settings. results include quality delta and cost delta.
11:12 Priya Rao: sounds good. we'll prepare a prompt sample.

11:22 Marcus Vela: security deep-dive: for SOC 2 we can share our latest report; for private deployment we support KMS integration and you get complete audit trail in your logging. for hosted, customer data is isolated per-tenant and retention policies configurable.
11:40 Marta Lin: retention policies — can we set 0 retention for prompts?
11:43 Marcus Vela: yes, retention is configurable per-workspace; you can disable storing prompts or keep only hashed metadata.

12:02 Marcus Vela: quick note on canary rollouts: you can pin a percent of traffic to new model and then rollback policy on error. this is useful when you test a new quantized variant.
12:16 Priya Rao: what's the SLA for dedicated pools? we need 99.9 for our service window.
12:21 Lena Park: Dedicated comes with an SLA — we'll include the SLA pdf in the followup.

12:38 Marcus Vela: back to the SDK details — error handling. transient 503s should be retried with exponential backoff; we expose typed errors in both sdks. also client has hooks for pre-request logging so your telemetry can correlate request ids.
12:55 Caleb Ortiz: do we get request ids that map to our logs?
12:58 Marcus Vela: yes each response includes x-redwood-request-id header. in private you can map that to your request trace id.

13:12 Marcus Vela: let's demo credentials rotation in node — small snippet using a callback that pulls from aws secrets manager, handles refresh, then sets the apiKey on client. (typing)
13:35 Priya Rao: (interrupt) that'll work, but we need an example that uses kubernetes service account chaining — any sample?
13:40 Marcus Vela: yes — sample in repo under ci/k8s-token-proxy.md; uses projected service account token to exchange for short-lived Redwood key.

13:59 Lena Park: jumping to summary and next steps. recap: we covered local and ci auth patterns, python and ts quickstarts, batching profile demo, console telemetry, security capabilities and Optimize evals. agreed POC: 2-week sandbox test on hosted with prompt set and locust harness, followed by dedicated sizing if results good.
14:22 Priya Rao: timeline looks fine. can we get cost estimate prior to the POC?
14:27 Lena Park: yes we'll send a cost estimate for hosted sandbox and a committed dedicated quote.
14:33 Marcus Vela: action items again: i'll prepare the POC runbook and attach locust script; lena will send pricing and sandbox creds; priya will share prompt set and CI secrets model; marta will list security questions for our SOC2 doc review.
14:46 Caleb Ortiz: one operational question — do you support A/B routing to multiple models for experiments?
14:50 Marcus Vela: yes — route config supports A/B and canary percentages, and the console shows per-model metrics.

15:03 Marta Lin: last question — is the sandbox data isolated from production logs?
15:07 Marcus Vela: yes sandbox is isolated and has short retention; production backups are separate.

15:20 Lena Park: ok thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the attachments and schedule the POC kickoff next week — propose monday 2025-03-24 at 15:00 UTC.
15:33 Priya Rao: that works. thanks lena, marcus.
15:36 Caleb Ortiz: thanks.
15:38 Marta Lin: thanks.
15:42 Meeting end.
